before: Interactive strategy environments require navigation services that respond to terrain changes while providing routes for many virtual agents. This study evaluates computational sharing across agents, reuse across environmental updates, and concurrency across independent workloads in six Unity navigation implementations. The evaluation combines dynamic planning, a matched cost and scaling benchmark, simulated movement, and managed worker scaling. In the original shared-goal planning acquisition, full-recompute and incremental flow fields achieved geometric mean handling times of 11.14 and 8.89 ms per scheduled event, compared with 52.48 ms for repeated A* and 59.55 ms for the frozen D* Lite implementation. A separate acquisition estimated 20.5% lower handling time for incremental repair across the fixed scenario matrix. In the matched experiment, incremental repair reduced adjusted geometric mean latency while increasing adjusted within-lane 95th-percentile latency by 11.9% and requiring approximately 2.42 times the model-adjusted retained planner state of full recomputation. Repeated A* and both flow fields completed all eight main movement conditions. Increasing from one to eight workers reduced private-batch time by 32.2–34.0% per doubling. These results identify complementary roles for shared computation, incremental repair, and workload concurrency, and guide navigation-backend selection according to goal structure, update demand, latency priorities, and memory capacity.
after: Interactive strategy environments require navigation services that respond to terrain changes while providing routes for many virtual agents. In the supplemental shared-goal acquisition with corrected D* Lite, full-recompute and incremental flow fields achieved geometric mean handling times of 10.78 and 8.72 ms per scheduled event, compared with 51.59 ms for repeated A* and 57.86 ms for D* Lite. A separate acquisition estimated 20.5% lower handling time for incremental repair across the fixed scenario matrix. In the matched experiment, incremental repair reduced adjusted geometric mean latency while increasing adjusted within-lane 95th-percentile latency by 11.9% and requiring approximately 2.42 times the model-adjusted retained planner state of full recomputation. Repeated A*, corrected D* Lite, and both flow fields completed all eight main movement conditions in the supplemental acquisition. Increasing from one to eight workers reduced private-batch time by 32.2–34.0% per doubling. These results identify complementary roles for shared computation, incremental repair, and workload concurrency, and guide navigation-backend selection according to goal structure, update demand, latency priorities, and memory capacity.

before: We compare repeated A* (A*-R), repeated bidirectional A* (BiA*-R), per-agent D* Lite (D*L), Lifelong Planning A* (LPA*), a full-recompute shared flow field (C-FF), and an incremental dynamic shared flow field (IDFF). The Unity framework provides common grids, planner operations, event schedules, and validation records. Four evaluation modules examine dynamic planning, matched computational costs, movement execution, and independent-workload concurrency. The dynamic-planning module contains three separately acquired studies, including a new-sample comparison of the two flow-field implementations.
after: We compare repeated A* (A*-R), repeated bidirectional A* (BiA*-R), per-agent D* Lite (D*L), Lifelong Planning A* (LPA*), a full-recompute shared flow field (C-FF), and an incremental dynamic shared flow field (IDFF). The Unity framework provides common grids, planner operations, event schedules, and validation records. Four evaluation modules examine dynamic planning, matched computational costs, movement execution, and independent-workload concurrency. The dynamic-planning module contains three initial acquisitions, including a field-confirmation study, and a supplemental acquisition with corrected D*L.

before: The dynamic-planning module contains three acquisitions. The four-method study evaluates A*-R, D*L, C-FF, and IDFF over 32 shared-goal campaigns with 48 paired blocks per campaign. Two additional heterogeneous-goal cohorts each contain 21 campaigns with 48 blocks: all queries retain assigned destinations, while the grouped-field implementations reject a query when its assigned goal differs from the field owner at its start. The expanded study measures BiA*-R, LPA*, C-FF, and IDFF together over the same 32 shared-goal scenarios in a new acquisition. The field-confirmation study acquires 50 new paired C-FF/IDFF blocks per scenario, balanced equally between execution orders. These acquisitions provide 10,176, 6,144, and 3,200 algorithm samples, respectively.
after: The historical dynamic-planning evidence comprises three acquisitions. The supplemental acquisition re-evaluated A*-R, corrected D*L, C-FF, and IDFF without pooling historical timings. Planning used 32 shared-goal scenarios × 48 four-algorithm Williams blocks (1,536 fresh Unity Editor processes; 6,144 samples). Movement repeated only the eight N = 128 main conditions in separate movement and callback lanes (768 fresh standalone-Player processes; 3,072 samples). The original analysis families and movement decision rule were retained. Supplementary Section S9 documents the implementation binding and results.

before: In the four-method study, the 32 campaign means supply the standard error; a normal approximation, Holm-adjusted tests [30], and Bonferroni intervals cover the five prespecified contrasts. Its interval quantifies repeat-run uncertainty for the fixed scenario matrix. Each acquisition is analyzed separately.

before: The three dynamic-planning acquisitions completed their planned samples. In the shared-goal four-method study, geometric mean P1 was 52.4800 ms per scheduled event for A*-R, 59.5523 for D*L, 11.1371 for C-FF, and 8.8945 for IDFF (Table 3). The simultaneous C-FF/A*-R ratio was 0.2122 (99% individual confidence interval 0.1199–0.3757; Holm-adjusted p = 5.47 × 10−12), and C-FF/D*L was 0.1870 (0.0807–0.4333; p = 2.75 × 10−7). IDFF/A*-R was 0.1695 (0.0867–0.3315; p = 1.40 × 10−11), and IDFF/D*L was 0.1494 (0.0924–0.2413; p = 4.54 × 10−24). Both shared-field implementations recorded lower dynamic handling times than the two per-agent backends in this acquisition; the D*L measurements include unsuccessful queries (Supplementary Section S2.5).
after: The supplemental four-method acquisition with corrected D*L completed all 1,536 paired blocks. Geometric mean P1 was 51.5919 ms per scheduled event for A*-R, 57.8581 for D*L, 10.7828 for C-FF, and 8.7185 for IDFF (Table 3). Each backend recorded 590,448 successful queries and 3,072 no-path outcomes, with zero failed, invalid, or budget-exceeded queries. C-FF/A*-R, C-FF/D*L, IDFF/A*-R, and IDFF/D*L ratios were 0.2090, 0.1864, 0.1690, and 0.1507, respectively; all four 99% individual Bonferroni intervals excluded one and all Holm-adjusted directional p values were below 0.001 (Supplementary Table S20). The IDFF/C-FF ratio was 0.8086 (99% individual interval 0.4670–1.4000; two-sided Holm p = 0.319), leaving that difference unresolved under the campaign-based analysis. Historical acquisitions remain separately identified.

before: A*-R, C-FF, and IDFF completed all agents in all 48 blocks of every main movement condition, with zero critical movement violations. Their simulated completion times were identical within each condition and ranged from 4.10 to 11.84 s (Table 5). D*L completed all agents in the four four-neighbor conditions, but failed all-agent completion in the four eight-neighbor conditions, covering 192 blocks. Those blocks contained 1,680 illegal_or_invalid_plan records, which combine unsuccessful planner status and adapter legality rejection.  Source-level replay reproduced the failed-agent identities and attributed the reproduced failures to premature termination of D*L repair under exact key comparison. The later tolerance-aware revision removed these failures in functional replay (Supplementary Section S3); the reported performance measurements remain those of the original build.
after: In the supplemental movement acquisition, all four implementations, including corrected D*L, completed every agent in all 48 blocks of each of the eight main conditions, with zero critical violations (Table 5). Their simulated completion times were identical within conditions and ranged from 4.10 to 11.84 s. All four passed the M3, M4 callback, and M5 eligibility gates. This resolves the historical D*L failure finding for the tested corrected implementation: the original acquisition had 192 incomplete blocks and 1,680 combined invalid-plan records. The source-level diagnosis and original outcomes remain in Supplementary Sections S3 and S9.

before: Each condition contains 48 paired blocks. M1 is simulation time in seconds; the 180 s D*L values are failure codes. before: The eligible A*-R, C-FF, and IDFF implementations had M1 ratios of 1.000000. The M2 ratio was 1.00002513 for A*-R against either field, while the C-FF/IDFF ratio was 1.00000000. Consequently, the movement rule selected no unique winner. The result shows that the measured planning-cost differences coexist with nearly identical path lengths and the same simulated completion times for these conditions. The 180 s D*L entries encode incomplete runs and are reported with their completion status.
after: All six eligible M1 pairwise ratios in the supplemental acquisition were 1.000000. The M2 ratio was 1.00000733 for A*-R against each other backend; D*L, C-FF, and IDFF had mutual ratios of 1.00000000. The retained deterministic zero-variance convention yields point intervals on these fixed inputs, not certainty for new maps. The original decision rule again selected no unique winner, now with all four backends eligible. The new common mask includes all agents, so its M2 values are not directly interchangeable with historical masked distances.

before: This study evaluates six navigation backends through dynamic planning, matched resource measurements, simulated movement, and independent-workload concurrency. Shared flow fields substantially reduce recorded dynamic handling time in the common-goal experiments. A separate acquisition estimates approximately 20.5% lower handling time for incremental repair relative to full recomputation across the fixed scenario matrix. The matched benchmark identifies the accompanying design trade-off: IDFF lowers adjusted geometric mean latency, grid access, and event-window allocation, while C-FF lowers adjusted P95 and retained state. A*-R and both fields complete all main movement conditions with identical simulated completion times. Managed workers reduce private-batch time by 32.2–34.0% per doubling, with further gains from eight to sixteen workers. Together, the results provide a quantitative basis for choosing navigation services according to shared-goal demand, update structure, latency priorities, and retained-state capacity in interactive strategy environments.
after: This study evaluates six navigation backends through dynamic planning, matched resource measurements, simulated movement, and independent-workload concurrency. The matched benchmark identifies the accompanying design trade-off: IDFF lowers adjusted geometric mean latency, grid access, and event-window allocation, while C-FF lowers adjusted P95 and retained state. A*-R, corrected D*L, and both fields complete all main movement conditions in the supplemental acquisition with identical simulated completion times and no unique winner. Managed workers reduce private-batch time by 32.2–34.0% per doubling, with further gains from eight to sixteen workers. Together, the results provide a quantitative basis for choosing navigation services according to shared-goal demand, update structure, latency priorities, and retained-state capacity in interactive strategy environments.

before: The historical repair loop compares priority keys exactly, although its g/rhs consistency test uses a 1e-12 tolerance. In a single-agent reproduction from core-r03-s1-shared (agent 55, start (63, 62), goal (14, 16)), the leading key differed by 1.42e-14 while the secondary key required further processing. Repair stopped and path extraction reached its step limit. The tolerance-aware revision (SHA-256 prefix b6938a3389de), already used by SMSB, changes only the two algorithm-control comparisons and their helper. With that revision, the eight movement replays produced 1,024 arrivals and zero InternalError results across 2,048 plan calls. In 53 fixed-start scenarios, the historical source reproduced all 335 failed query identities sampled across the scenarios, whose per-scenario status totals were identical over all 48 archived repetitions. The corrected source reduced InternalError from 335 to zero across 21,325 calls; successes increased from 20,954 to 21,261 and no-path results from 36 to 64. All 64 corrected no-path query identities matched archived A*-R results, and all returned successful paths passed legality checks. These functional checks ran under the installed Unity distribution's Mono runtime using the frozen scenario, grid, event and movement logic. They do not constitute a new standalone-Player performance acquisition or a full optimal-cost oracle test. The historical Player binary was unavailable at its recorded path, so the original timing results and their implementation identity remain unchanged.
